issues.item: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner', the appraisal 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' is clinically hard to reconcile because this trauma does not ordinarily involve other deaths or a mass-casualty context. The rest of the profile centers on partner violence, hypervigilance, and fragmented visual recall, so this item introduces a markedly different trauma scenario without support elsewhere in the selected items.

'Car sounds' is difficult to connect clinically to the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The other trigger items and all threat, memory, and appraisal items center on interpersonal trauma, bodily alarm, betrayal, and fragmented terror-based recall. A car-sound trigger suggests a different trauma context unless there is supporting material elsewhere, so this item is the main coherence concern.

vignette: Rohan's eyes scan the crowded coffee shop, his mind on high alert for any signs of danger. It's been three years since his ex-partner's abuse ended, but the memories still linger, and the smallest triggers can send him spiraling back into a state of hypervigilance. The sound of incomprehensible chatter, like the cacophony of voices in this coffee shop, is enough to make him feel on edge. His body reacts before his mind has a chance to catch up, his heart racing and muscles tensing as if preparing for a fight. As he waits in line, Rohan catches a whiff of alcohol from the barista's breath. The smell transports him back to that fateful night when his ex-partner, drunk and angry, had attacked him. The memory is vivid, like a snapshot in his mind – he remembers the feeling of terror, the sound of shattering glass, and the pain of his partner's blows. Remembering it brings back the same fear he felt at the time, making it difficult for him to breathe. Rohan's experiences have left him with deep-seated self-doubt. He can't trust that he'll do the right thing, especially when it comes to relationships. He feels like he failed in his most important role as a partner and husband. The betrayal cuts deep – how could someone he loved and trusted hurt him so badly? These negative appraisals swirl in his mind, making it hard for him to shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge. As an architect, Rohan's work requires attention to detail and creativity, but lately, he finds himself struggling to focus. The slightest noise or movement makes him jump, and he has difficulty falling asleep at night, always staying alert in case something happens. His body is constantly reacting to perceived threats, making it hard for him to relax. The memories of the abuse continue to haunt Rohan, especially when triggered by specific sights, sounds, or smells. When these memories resurface, they bring back the terror he felt during the event, and his mind starts racing with worst-case scenarios. This hyperarousal makes it even more difficult for him to shake off the feeling of being in danger. As Rohan navigates his daily life, he becomes increasingly withdrawn. He avoids social gatherings and public places, fearing that something might trigger another flashback or anxiety attack. His relationships suffer as a result – his wife feels like she's losing her husband to the past, and Rohan feels like he's failing her all over again. Despite his best efforts, Rohan can't seem to escape the cycle of fear and hypervigilance. He knows he needs help but is terrified of facing the memories and emotions head-on. The thought of therapy is daunting, but he hopes that by confronting his demons, he might finally find some peace and learn to trust himself again.
